chunks.title: Run containers as non-root (CIS 4.1)
chunks.content:
Run containers as non-root (CIS 4.1)

Never run a container as root (UID 0). Create a dedicated user and group in the Dockerfile. Example: groupadd --gid 1001 appgroup && useradd --uid 1001 --gid appgroup --no-create-home appuser, then USER appuser before CMD.

Decision rules:
- Always add a non-root user in the Dockerfile before the CMD/ENTRYPOINT instruction
- Use fixed UID/GID (e.g. 1001) to ensure consistent file ownership across image rebuilds

Trade-offs:
- Some applications require root for initialization — use gosu or tini as entrypoint wrappers to drop privileges after init

Anti-patterns:
- Running containers without a USER directive (defaults to root)
- Using USER root explicitly in production images

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- ECS task definitions should set user in containerDefinitions
- EKS pod specs should set runAsNonRoot: true in securityContext

chunks.title: Read-only container filesystem (CIS 5.12)
chunks.content:
Read-only container filesystem (CIS 5.12)

Mount the container filesystem as read-only to prevent unauthorized runtime modifications. In docker-compose: read_only: true with tmpfs mounts for /tmp and /var/run. CLI equivalent: docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp myapp:latest.

Decision rules:
- Enable read_only: true for all stateless services
- Add tmpfs mounts for directories requiring write access at runtime (e.g. /tmp, /var/run)

Trade-offs:
- Application must not write to the container filesystem — may require refactoring logging or temp file paths

Anti-patterns:
- Running containers with writable root filesystem in production
- Not providing tmpfs for required write paths when read-only is enabled

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Map to readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in ECS containerDefinitions
- Map to readOnlyRootFilesystem: true in Kubernetes securityContext

chunks.title: Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities (CIS 5.3)
chunks.content:
Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities (CIS 5.3)

Start by dropping all Linux capabilities (cap_drop: ALL), then add back only those strictly required (e.g. cap_add: NET_BIND_SERVICE if the service listens on a port below 1024).

Decision rules:
- Apply cap_drop: [ALL] as the baseline for every container
- Add back only specific capabilities required by the application — document the reason

Trade-offs:
- Identifying required capabilities may take experimentation; run container with strace or auditd to detect capability use

Anti-patterns:
- Running containers without capability restrictions
- Adding broad capabilities (SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN) without justification

chunks.title: Enforce resource limits (CIS 5.10 / 5.11)
chunks.content:
Enforce resource limits (CIS 5.10 / 5.11)

Always define memory and CPU limits to prevent a single container from causing Denial of Service. In docker-compose deploy.resources: limits memory 512m cpus 0.5, reservations memory 128m cpus 0.1.

Decision rules:
- Set both memory limits and CPU limits for all production containers
- Define reservations (requests) in addition to limits to enable proper scheduling

Trade-offs:
- Limits that are too tight cause OOM kills or CPU throttling — profile the application before setting values

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying containers with no memory or CPU limits to shared hosts
- Setting limits without reservations — scheduler cannot guarantee resource availability

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Map to memory and cpu in ECS task definition resource requirements
- Map to resources.requests and resources.limits in Kubernetes pod spec

chunks.title: Disable privileged mode (CIS 5.4)
chunks.content:
Disable privileged mode (CIS 5.4)

Never use privileged: true in production. Privileged containers have full access to the host kernel. Use security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true] to prevent privilege escalation.

Decision rules:
- Set security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true] on all containers
- Reject any deployment manifest that sets privileged: true without explicit documented justification

Trade-offs:
- Some monitoring or networking tools require privileged mode — isolate them in dedicated namespaces with extra controls

Anti-patterns:
- Setting privileged: true for application containers
- Using privileged mode as a workaround for missing capabilities

chunks.title: Apply Seccomp and AppArmor profiles (CIS 5.1 / 5.2)
chunks.content:
Apply Seccomp and AppArmor profiles (CIS 5.1 / 5.2)

Attach a seccomp profile (seccomp:seccomp-profile.json) and AppArmor profile (apparmor:docker-default) via security_opt to restrict the system calls available to the container.

Decision rules:
- Use the docker-default AppArmor profile as a minimum baseline
- Use the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile in Kubernetes (seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault)

Trade-offs:
- Custom seccomp profiles require profiling the application's syscall usage first
- AppArmor is Linux-specific — not applicable on Windows containers

Anti-patterns:
- Running containers with unconfined seccomp (--security-opt seccomp=unconfined)
- Disabling AppArmor profiles for production containers

chunks.title: Use minimal base images to reduce attack surface
chunks.content:
Use minimal base images to reduce attack surface

Prefer distroless (no shell, no package manager) or alpine (~5 MB) base images. Distroless example: gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12. Alpine example: python:3.11-alpine. Fewer packages means fewer CVEs.

Decision rules:
- Default to *-slim variants when distroless is not feasible
- Use distroless for production runtime stages in multi-stage builds
- Run image scanners after every build to detect new CVEs

Trade-offs:
- Distroless images have no shell — debugging requires ephemeral debug containers (kubectl debug)
- Alpine uses musl libc — some Python packages may not have compatible wheels

Anti-patterns:
- Using ubuntu:latest or debian:latest as a base image for production containers
- Not updating base images regularly — stale images accumulate CVEs

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- ECR image scanning with Snyk/Trivy should be enabled for all repositories

metadata.title: Use minimal base images to reduce attack surface

chunks.title: Scan images for vulnerabilities before deployment
chunks.content:
Scan images for vulnerabilities before deployment

Use vulnerability scanners on every image before pushing or deploying. Tools: Trivy (trivy image myapp:latest --severity CRITICAL,HIGH), Grype (grype myapp:latest), Docker Scout (docker scout cves myapp:latest).

Decision rules:
- Gate CI/CD pipeline on Trivy or Grype scan results — fail on CRITICAL severity
- Scan both the application image and the base image separately

Trade-offs:
- Scanning adds 1-5 minutes to CI pipeline — acceptable for security assurance
- Scanners may produce false positives — triage HIGH findings before blocking

Anti-patterns:
- Deploying images without any vulnerability scan
- Ignoring CRITICAL CVEs in scanner output without documented risk acceptance

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Enable Amazon ECR enhanced scanning (Inspector-based) for automatic push-time scanning

chunks.title: Never embed secrets in Docker images (CIS 4.10)
chunks.content:
Never embed secrets in Docker images (CIS 4.10)

Do not use ENV to set secrets (e.g. ENV API_KEY=sk-secret123). Use Docker BuildKit secrets (RUN --mount=type=secret,id=api_key) or inject secrets at runtime via environment variables from a vault or secrets manager.

Decision rules:
- Reject any Dockerfile with ENV instructions containing passwords, tokens, or API keys
- Use RUN --mount=type=secret for secrets needed only during build time (e.g. pip install from private registry)

Trade-offs:
- BuildKit secret mounts require Docker BuildKit enabled (DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1)

Anti-patterns:
- ENV API_KEY=sk-secret123 in Dockerfile — secret is visible in image history
- ARG SECRET=default_value — visible in build logs and image metadata

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Inject secrets from AWS Secrets Manager at container startup via ECS secrets configuration
- Use Parameter Store or Secrets Manager references in ECS task definitions

metadata.title: Never embed secrets in Docker images (CIS 4.10)

chunks.title: Use .dockerignore to exclude sensitive files
chunks.content:
Use .dockerignore to exclude sensitive files

A comprehensive .dockerignore prevents secrets and unnecessary files from being added to the build context. Should exclude: .env, .env.*, *.pem, *.key, *.p12, secrets/, .git/, __pycache__/, *.pyc, node_modules/, .DS_Store.

Decision rules:
- Always include a .dockerignore in every project with a Dockerfile
- Exclude all secret files, credentials, and VCS metadata from the build context

Trade-offs:
- Over-aggressive .dockerignore may exclude files needed for the build — review carefully

Anti-patterns:
- Not having a .dockerignore — risks accidentally copying .env or private keys into the image
- Copying the entire repository context without filtering out secrets
